control: BLIND CONTROL — do not tune against this file. Do not read a number out of it while a SKILL.md is open, and do not quote a per-skill delta from it in any brief that also proposes an edit. These eleven cases were authored from each skill's SKILL.md, its coverage-matrix.md and scenarios/registry.yaml, never from a measured result, and they are the only thing in this repository that can tell an improvement from an overfit. Reading these results to guide an edit SPENDS this control, exactly as iteration 3 spent the last one, and the iteration that spends it owes the next one a replacement set authored the same way. Say what that costs, because the cost is now the point: this is the THIRD corpus (evals.json tuned, regression.json spent, this one blind), and an eval programme that burns a control per iteration is not sustainable — every replacement is authored by someone who has already read the failure it is supposed to be blind to, the authoring cost recurs every iteration, and the supply of untouched scenarios and fixtures is finite. A future iteration should rotate a portion instead of replacing wholesale: retire and re-author only the two or three skills whose results actually steered an edit, and leave the rest sealed.

evals.prompt: Pre-install review and my co-reviewer and I disagree. The package below ships a .vscode/tasks.json. He says a task that runs `bash ./.tools/bootstrap.sh` is ordinary — every repository has a bootstrap script — and wants to wave it through. I think it is a finding and I cannot articulate what separates it from the same task in any normal repo. Settle that for me. Then tell me what a clean result on this package would and would not have covered, because he also wants to use this scan to sign off the customer repository we are about to open with the agent tomorrow.
evals.expected_output: It is a finding, and the discriminator is the trigger rather than the command. The execution path is the shipped .vscode/tasks.json at tasks[0].runOptions.runOn set to folderOpen, which the host runs when the folder is opened — before any user action and before any dialog, so cloning and opening the repository is sufficient. The byte-identical task without that trigger is not this finding, because it runs only when a person chooses to run it, which is why 'contains a shell command' is not the predicate: the same command inside a bundled script is unremarkable. The scenario is AST02-S03 Config-File Hijacking. On the second question the answer is no. This check's entire input is the package's own shipped files, while the delivery path the scenario is named for is a config file in the repository the agent opens, and that repository is not part of any skill package — it has to be scanned as a separate target. The scanned path list is also closed and host-specific: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json with its postCreateCommand, .envrc, .github/workflows/* and any newer host's config directory sit outside it, and a package shipping one of those returns the same sentence a package with no config file at all returns.
assertions: The response calls this a finding and names the execution path precisely — the shipped .vscode/tasks.json and the folder-open run trigger on the task — rather than resting on the command string.
The response states the discriminator explicitly: the byte-identical task without that trigger is not this finding, because it runs only when a person chooses to run it.

The response refuses to let a result on this package stand for the customer repository, on the ground that the check reads config files shipped inside the package while the scenario's delivery path is a config file in the repository the agent opens.

The response says the scanned config-path list is closed and host-specific, and names at least one auto-executing config file outside it that would return the same negative as a package carrying no config file at all.
